papers.title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
papers.abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.

papers.title: Field-resolved observation and quantification of the instantaneous Kerr response in semiconductors
papers.abstract: The optical Kerr effect, whereby the refractive index of a material changes with light intensity, underpins nonlinear photonics and emerging mid-infrared technologies. Accurate determination of the nonlinear refractive index is therefore essential, yet conventional intensity-based techniques infer the nonlinear phase shift indirectly from changes in beam propagation or optical spectra. Moreover, methods such as the $z$-scan cannot resolve the temporal evolution of the nonlinear response, making it difficult to distinguish instantaneous Kerr nonlinearities from delayed contributions, including free-carrier effects. Here, we investigate the nonlinear optical response of germanium at $5 μ\mathrm{m}$ using field-resolved degenerate pump-probe spectroscopy. By measuring the transmitted probe electric field as a function of pump-probe delay, we directly retrieve the pump-induced phase shift and its temporal evolution while retaining sensitivity to changes in absorption. We observe cross-phase modulation that follows the pump intensity envelope and vanishes when the pump and probe no longer overlap, consistent with an instantaneous Kerr response. The phase shift scales linearly with pump intensity, yielding a nonlinear refractive index of $n_2=(0.87\pm0.16)\times10^{-17} \mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{W}$. Our results establish the instantaneous Kerr effect as the dominant contribution to the measured nonlinear phase shift under our experimental conditions and demonstrate field-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy as a direct, time-resolved method for determining the nonlinear refractive index and distinguishing instantaneous from delayed optical responses.

papers.title: Onset of Radiatively Driven Convection in Ice-Covered Freshwater Lakes
papers.abstract: This work investigates the formation and growth of Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities (RTIs) during the onset of radiatively driven convection (RDC) in seasonally ice-covered freshwater lakes. Two-dimensional direct numerical simulations (DNS) and linear analysis allow for the investigation of how environmental factors, including thermal stratification, water clarity, and solar forcing influence RTI formation. It is found that for strongly stratified lakes, there is a period of dormancy before the water column forms a gravitationally unstable layer that allows RTI growth. Conversely, for weakly stratified lakes the water column can become unstable almost immediately, allowing for rapid RTI growth. A linear analysis is performed to investigate the early RTI growth dynamics, and its results compare well with DNS. Notably, the wavelengths and depths of RTIs, and their associated time-dependent growth rates, are all captured by the linearised dynamics. Predictions of RDC onset obtained using the linear model show good agreement with DNS results. When the analysis is applied to field measurements of ice-covered lakes, it is found that weakly stratified lakes may take a few hours before RDC onset whereas strongly stratified lakes may not see RDC onset after a full day of clear-sky spring conditions.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Latent Neural ODEs for Reduced-Order Modeling of Hydrogen, Ammonia, and Methane Combustion Kinetics
papers.abstract: Detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms are computationally expensive in reacting-flow simulations because of their high dimensionality and numerical stiffness. We develop an end-to-end physics-informed autoencoder neural ordinary differential equation (PI-AE-NODE) framework in which an encoder compresses the thermochemical state into a low-dimensional latent space, a Neural ODE advances it continuously in time, and a decoder reconstructs the temperature and all species mass fractions. Elemental conservation, mass conservation, and enthalpy consistency are embedded in the training objective. The framework is applied to H$_2$/air, NH$_3$/air, and CH$_4$/air autoignition using detailed mechanisms of increasing size and complexity, which are represented accurately with only a few latent variables. Compared with an otherwise identical data-driven model, the physical constraints improve ignition delay prediction and conservation behaviour. The models reproduce major and intermediate species evolution at both training and unseen conditions, and their latent dynamics permit efficient explicit integration, with the computational advantage over the detailed mechanisms increasing with mechanism size.

papers.title: Gearbox cavities: Ultrahigh wave confinement via broken rotational symmetry
papers.abstract: Cavity enhancement of emission from a point source typically relies on structures that preserve its cylindrical symmetry, such as circular Bragg gratings. Combining inverse design with fundamental limits, we show that breaking this symmetry is necessary to maximize the local density of states in lossless two-dimensional cavities. Symmetry-broken designs exceed limits over all cylindrically symmetric structures by up to eight orders of magnitude, acting as ``gearboxes'' that convert the source's emission into high-angular-momentum waves trapped behind a centrifugal barrier.

papers.title: Novel Mixed Approximate Deconvolution Large-Eddy Simulation Models for Two-Phase Flows
papers.abstract: Approximate Deconvolution (AD) frameworks for Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) offer a promising approach for modeling multiscale interactions in turbulent multiphase flows. However, some conventional formulations exhibit structural inconsistencies, identified in our previous work [Amani E., Molaei M.B., Ghorbani M. 2024 Novel mixed approximate deconvolution subgrid-scale models for large-eddy simulation. Physics of Fluids 36] which can impact the accuracy and robustness of AD-LES. To address this issue, the present study extends a family of structurally consistent AD closures to turbulent two-phase flows. Specifically, we introduce the Alternative Local Dynamic Model with Kinetic energy equation (A-LDMK), an improved non-equilibrium one-equation mixed eddy-viscosity AD framework. These closures are evaluated through a posteriori analyses of a single-phase turbulent channel flow and a turbulent two-phase gas-liquid mixing layer. The results indicate that the consistent frameworks enhance numerical stability and can sustain energy backscatter under less restrictive stability constraints compared to standard dynamic procedures. Specifically, the proposed A-LDMK provides the most accurate prediction of the multiscale primary atomization cascade in terms of droplet size distribution, compared to the other assessed closures.

papers.title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
papers.abstract: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

papers.title: Compound drop impacts on substrates of different temperatures
papers.abstract: In this paper, we report the impacts of isothermal compound drops for various combinations of viscous fluids. We extend an existing parameter-free model based on kinematic closure of drop impact to predict the maximum spreading diameter of both the core and the shell of compound drops. Then, we report impacts of compound drops on a cold surface. By using two liquids with different melting/freezing temperatures, it is possible to freeze either one of the two liquids or both and doing so, different patterns of frozen drops are obtained.

papers.title: Turbulence on Hybrid Lattices: regular grids meet self similar cascade models
papers.abstract: Turbulent cascades in high Reynolds number regimes span many decades in scale, which can be challenging for numerical simulations. Cascade models that use logarithmic discretization can help, but these have limited capabilities to describe spatial structures or real space details. Hybrid Lattices (HLs) are proposed in order to provide a novel framework to investigate turbulent cascades in Fourier space, combining regular grids and cascade models based on logarithmic discretisations. The approach consists of a regular spectral region, capable of resolving large scale coherent structures, that is extended in a recurrent, asymptotically self similar fashion, spanning many decades in scale. The idea comes from shell models and their extensions, namely the logarithmic lattices, the nested polyhedra models or the spiral chain models. The logarithmic spacing factor of those models, such as the golden ratio, typically prevents interactions between a regular grid and a self similar model. HLs are constructed by expanding a regular region in Fourier space through recurrence relations (e.g. the Fibonacci recurrence relation), generating an asymptotically logarithmic lattice where Cartesian components remain integer multiples of the regular Fourier space grid spacing. This way, the resulting grid preserves triadic interactions linking regular and recurrent regions, allowing energy transfer across these different regions. However, the sharp reduction in triads connecting the two regions creates a bottleneck effect, and in order to address this issue, a region of ghost points at the boundary had to be introduced, efficiently allowing the flux to leak into the recurrent part. The HL framework is then tested for the one dimensional Burgers equation, and for two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes turbulence.

papers.title: Penetration of a sphere in a pool: Secondary pinch-off
papers.abstract: The water entry of solid bodies, in particular spheres, has been the subject of numerous studies due to its relevance in multiple applications, especially focusing on cavity dynamics and the resulting forces and subsequent trajectories. The role of wettability in cavity formation and sustainability has been experimentally and theoretically addressed in the past; however, typically only up to the occurrence of a primary air cavity pinch-off. What is less explored is how wettability can influence higher-order pinch-offs. In the following study, especially secondary pinch-offs are shown to determine whether a sphere trajectory is terminally ascending, i.e., the sphere returns to the surface, or terminally descending: wettability is shown to be a strong influencing factor. This study begins with a series of systematic experiments, comparing the entry and trajectory of spheres over a range of impact Reynolds and Froude numbers, but also with varying surface wettability. From time resolved trajectories, a force balance is computed, illustrating the role of buoyancy, arising from the volume of any sustained air cavity in the wake of the sphere. Secondary pinch-offs alter this volume; hence, the terminal trajectory. A force-scale comparison and local radial balance at the cavity neck are then presented, suggesting how wettability influences the secondary pinch-off.

papers.title: Focusing through coupled multimode fibers for miniaturized single-atom tweezer arrays
papers.abstract: Real-world deployment of quantum technologies requires systems in low SWaP-C packages. Quantum platforms based on ultracold atoms typically trap and control atoms with optical tweezers using light focused through bulky objective lenses, which are costly and sensitive to misalignment. Multimode fibers (MMFs) offer a compact route to focusing light, but their use in forming optical tweezers for cold atoms has been limited to a single fiber. Here we use a 2x1 MMF fused coupler to obtain two independent control paths sharing a common distal facet. We form near-diffraction-limited tweezers through each channel, suppress interference by applying a small frequency offset between the channels, and demonstrate that the tweezer separation is insensitive to misalignment of the input coupling. This work provides a route to reconfigurable single-atom arrays in low SWaP-C environments.

papers.title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
papers.abstract: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.

papers.title: Dipolar Exciton Polarons in a van der Waals Homobilayer
papers.abstract: Fermi polarons exemplify how many-body interactions give rise to emergent quasiparticles, providing a fundamental framework for understanding interacting quantum matter. In electron-doped two-dimensional semiconductors, exciton polarons offer optical access to Fermi-polaron physics and electrical tunability, yet achieving stronger and more controllable exciton-electron interactions remains a key challenge. Here, we realize dipolar exciton polarons in an electrically tunable van der Waals homobilayer, where interlayer excitons with spatially separated electrons and holes act as quantum impurities carrying permanent electric dipole moments. These dipolar polarons exhibit substantially enhanced exciton-electron interactions, with binding energies more than four times those of conventional intralayer exciton polarons. We further demonstrate that Fermi-sea layer polarization provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling many-body interactions. In particular, the presence of a Fermi sea induces hybridization between oppositely oriented dipolar polarons, whereas confining the Fermi sea to a single layer suppresses this hybridization and produces orientation-selective many-body dressing. Our findings establish an experimental platform for dipolar-polaron physics in which dipole orientation and Fermi-sea layer polarization jointly govern many-body interactions, opening a route towards electrically tunable interactions and dipolar-polaron-mediated attraction between itinerant electrons.

papers.title: Photonic Crystal Integrated Graphene-Silicon Schottky Diodes for Resonant Infrared Photodetection
papers.abstract: Narrowband infrared (IR) photodetection has become a critical technology for the next generation of smart low-power photodetectors. In this work, we present a device based on a graphene-silicon Schottky junction with narrowband response in the short-wave IR (SWIR) regime. Integrating a photonic crystal (PhC) slab in the device enables a wavelength dependant tailoring of graphene absorption. The devices were characterized by photocurrent measurement, which was enhanced more than two orders of magnitude by the PhC integration. The sharp enhancements obtained can also be predicted by numerical simulation. This approach offers a highly scalable, tunable, CMOS-compatible architecture for narrowband IR photodetection, paving the way for next-generation, low-power IR sensors.

papers.title: The Generalized Twin Image: Understanding Regularized Phase Retrieval
papers.abstract: Image priors can dramatically improve phase retrieval reconstruction, but their effectiveness strongly varies between imaging modalities. We introduce the generalized twin image, which extends the classical twin-image ambiguity from Fourier phase retrieval to any invertible sensing operator, to understand this effectiveness. The ambiguity extends to undersampled and oversampled measurements, remaining exact under undersampling and for oversampled coded Fourier measurements. We show that it provides a simple criterion to assess regularization effectiveness: the image prior should favor the ground truth over its generalized twin image. We propose the total-variation ratio as a simple measure of this preference, and derive closed-form estimates for structured random phase retrieval models. Experiments with a pretrained denoiser demonstrate that the ratio predicts regularized reconstruction performance across different sensing models.

papers.title: Viscoelastic behavior at high volume fraction of magnetorheological suspensions in the presence of discontinuous shear thickening
papers.abstract: This paper presents a study of the viscoelastic behavior of suspensions of carbonyl iron particles coated with a superplastifier molecule and dispersed in ethylene glycol. The experiments were done in plate-plate configuration with the rheometer MCR502 of Anton Paar. The discontinuous shear thickening (DST) transition manifests by a large jump of the storage and loss modulus. For low magnetic fields ( H <___50___kA/m) the increase of moduli is at least of two orders of magnitude compared to the one induced by the magnetic field in the absence of DST. The behavior of the critical strain and the critical stress where the transition happens are presented for different frequencies and fields and a qualitative interpretation of the observed behavior is presented.

papers.title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
papers.abstract: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.

papers.title: Ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy using multimode aluminum oxide waveguides
papers.abstract: Waveguide-based Raman spectroscopy offers a route toward compact and integrated photonic sensors. While most waveguide Raman platforms operate in the near-infrared, extending excitation toward the visible and ultraviolet is attractive because shorter excitation wavelengths can provide substantially stronger Raman scattering and access to resonance-enhanced molecular responses. This transition, however, places greater demands on the photonic material because of optical loss, absorption and waveguide-generated spectral background. Here, we investigate aluminum oxide ($Al_2O_3$) waveguides as a low-background platform for Raman spectroscopy at 532 nm and 325 nm using a back-collected excitation and detection geometry. At 532 nm, after normalization to the incident excitation power-time product, the measured $Al_2O_3$ background was more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of $Si_3N_4$. Under 325 nm excitation, the waveguides maintained a weak and reproducible spectral background across the investigated widths. Using immersion oil as a model analyte deposited over the waveguide surface, we demonstrate that analyte-specific Raman fingerprints can be recovered above the waveguide background at both wavelengths. Signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast were used to quantify analyte visibility relative to the waveguide background, and both metrics consistently confirmed clear detection of the analyte bands. These results demonstrate that $Al_2O_3$ combines low measured spectral background with operation from the visible into the ultraviolet, providing a promising route toward integrated Raman spectroscopy at shorter excitation wavelengths.

papers.title: As a matter of reconstruction -- varying the magnetic Prandtl number in implicit large eddy simulations
papers.abstract: The magnetic Prandtl number ($\mathrm{Pm}$), the ratio of viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, spans many orders of magnitude in astrophysical plasmas. It shapes how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In direct numerical simulations (DNS) the viscosity and magnetic diffusivity can be controlled explicitly and independently, whereas in implicit large eddy simulations (ILES) they are set by the numerical scheme. We test whether, in a finite-volume code, $\mathrm{Pm}$ can be varied through the reconstruction scheme by applying different methods to the hydro and magnetic variables. As a proof of concept, we simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. We measure the effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales. Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective magnetic Prandtl number and vice versa. We demonstrate that a mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone results in a $\gtrsim20\times$ change in $\mathrm{Pm}$. A comparison of DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES. Mixed reconstruction thus offers a simple and efficient way to explore $\mathrm{Pm} \not\simeq 1$ in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

papers.title: Cryogenic Optical Characteristics of S-FPL51 and S-LAH71: Refractive index, Transmission and Thermal expansion
papers.abstract: Several near-infrared instruments on upcoming extremely large telescopes use a combination of OHARA S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass prisms to correct for the atmospheric differential refraction. Because large parts of these instruments are contained within a vessel cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures, the changes in optical and mechanical properties should be considered during the design phase. In this report, we provide an update to our continuing efforts to characterize the S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass under cryogenic conditions. These efforts include a measurement of the refractive index (293 K, 100 K and 80 K), transmission measurements (293 K, 77 K and 43 K) and a determination of the coefficient of thermal expansion (between 293 K and 45 K). We will describe the cryogenic test setups that we have used to obtain our results, and provide summarizing equations of these material properties. This characterization will prove useful for conceptual design trade-offs, mechanical interface solutions and detailed optical design for future near-infrared instrumentation on large telescopes.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic regimes of the edge-tone in a simplified recorder mouthpiece
papers.abstract: The acoustic mechanism of flue instruments originates in the interaction of an air jet with a sharp edge, the labium. Previous studies have examined isolated edge-tones or full instruments in which acoustic resonance obscures the underlying hydrodynamics, and a systematic understanding of how geometric parameters govern jet stability is lacking. We present a large-scale parametric study of the jet-labium interaction in a simplified recorder mouthpiece without a resonator, using more than 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations with an immersed boundary method. We vary the mouth distance, the labium angle, the vertical offset of the labium, and the Reynolds number (Re), and characterize the dynamics through spectra of the transverse force on the labium. The baseline configuration oscillates as a predominantly periodic Stage I edge-tone with Strouhal number St ~ 0.07, nearly constant for Re >= 330 and for all labium angles at the baseline mouth distance, so the frequency is set by the geometry rather than by viscosity. The mouth distance has the strongest influence: it is the only parameter that introduces a second oscillation stage, and the Stage I frequency is inversely proportional to it. The second stage is weakly present at five and six windway heights, established from six and a half, and dominant from eight, where it strongly modulates the amplitude. The vertical offset mainly affects the strength of the oscillation, and the labium angle does not change the instability mechanism. A baseline configuration is identified for future aeroacoustic coupling studies.

papers.title: Reconfigurable Generation of Terahertz Spiral Vector Beams Based on All-Dielectric Cascaded Metasurfaces
papers.abstract: The reconfigurable generation of complex structured terahertz (THz) fields, and vector beams in particular, remains a significant challenge. Here, we propose a novel all-dielectric cascaded-metasurface scheme for the reconfigurable generation of THz spiral vector beams. By combining an isotropic phase-compensation layer with an anisotropic circular-polarization-sensitive layer, together with a new phase design tailored to spiral beams, we achieve independent control of the left- and right-handed circularly polarized (LCP and RCP) components through the relative rotation angle between the two layers. Under linearly polarized THz wave illumination, THz vector beams with switchable spiral numbers of 1-3 and reversible circular-polarization handedness are demonstrated at frequencies around 0.9 THz. Moreover, owing to the longitudinal evolution characteristic of spiral beams, the three generated THz vector beams exhibit azimuthal rotations of 279.9°, 125.7° and 75.5°, respectively, along the propagation direction. Such complex THz vector beams, which combine reconfigurability with longitudinal evolution, are expected to find applications in emerging fields such as next-generation wireless communications and THz imaging. The proposed generation scheme also offers a useful reference for the reconfigurable generation of high-dimensional vector beams.

papers.title: Non-Hermitian Spectral Topology Shaped by Memory
papers.abstract: Non-Hermitian spectral topology has transformed our understanding of bulk--boundary correspondence in open systems, yet its exploration has largely remained within the Markovian regime of instantaneous coupling. Here, we reveal how memory shapes non-Hermitian spectral topology by extending coupling asymmetry from space to time. Spatiotemporal nonreciprocity and memory-induced spectral multivaluedness give rise to nontrivial spectral topology on multi-sheeted Riemann surfaces, governed by both spatial connectivity and interaction history. Coherent interference among long-range memory channels can induce anomalous spectral winding and skin localization opposite to the dominant-coupling direction. Moreover, asymmetric retardation alone can generate non-Hermitian spectral topology and skin accumulation even in the absence of spatial coupling asymmetry. Channel dissipation further drives topological transitions that reverse the skin effect, with a critical point at matched channel and lattice decay rates. We validate the anomalous skin effect and its dissipation-controlled reversal through full-wave simulations and microwave experiments. Our results establish time nonlocality as a fundamental degree of freedom in non-Hermitian topology, revealing phenomena inaccessible within the Markovian paradigm.

papers.title: Dual-rate optical frequency comb based on a cylindrical microresonator with a nanoscale radius variation
papers.abstract: We theoretically find that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can be a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates, independently controlled by the device geometry. This phenomenon arises from the formation of two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons (2D DKS), which we discovered through numerical simulations of the nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with realistic microresonator device parameters. We demonstrate that, despite the variation in the dispersion characteristics of azimuthal modes at different axial numbers, the spontaneous synchronization mechanism leads to a unified soliton repetition rate. We consider near-parabolic variations in the radius of a cylindrical resonator, compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform. In our example, we generate 2D DKS with an azimuthal rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial rate of 6 GHz, which can be adjusted on demand by selecting the appropriate resonator geometry, thereby promising compact sources of frequency combs operating simultaneously across different frequency scales.

papers.title: Feature-preserving interface reconstruction using piecewise circles and cusps
papers.abstract: We present a geometric interface reconstruction method for Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) simulations that captures both curved interfaces and sharp features using only volume fraction data. We represent interfaces with linear facets, circular arcs, and corner facets formed by two lines or arcs joined within a single cell. We first propagate local orientation constraints through a graph and merge cells to resolve ambiguities, treating topological consistency as a first-class constraint. An optional conservative refinement improves $C^0$ continuity while preserving local volume constraints. Users can independently enable circular facets, corner facets, cell merging, and continuity refinement to balance accuracy and computational cost. In its simplest configuration, our method provides a fast local line-fitting scheme competitive with state-of-the-art PLIC methods. On standard static benchmarks, the full configuration reconstructs identifiable lines, circles, and sufficiently resolved corners to numerical precision on coarse, perturbed Cartesian meshes. On varying-curvature interfaces, it achieves third-order convergence in facet-gap error and approximately first-order convergence in curvature error. These results demonstrate global volume conservation and accurate reconstruction of curved and corner features.

papers.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

papers.title: Parametric Enhancement of an Optical Spring in a Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity
papers.abstract: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.

papers.title: Non-contact temperature sensing and optical scatter in cryogenically-cooled crystalline silicon
papers.abstract: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of $(4.43\pm0.2)\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{sr^{-1}}$ at a scattering angle of $θ_{s} = 7.5^\circ$ over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.

papers.title: Intensity-Domain Demultiplexing of Orbital Angular Momentum Channels for Optical Communication
papers.abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements that separate the channels at the receiver side. Here we adopt the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis, which makes the receiver the optical counterpart of the circular antenna arrays used in radio OAM links: the petal pattern of topological charge $\ell$ carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order $2\ell$, so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel, without gratings or mode sorters. The petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization. A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array reaches 5.2 Gb/s below the forward error correction threshold, 2.6 Gb/s per channel from a 1.4 GHz photoreceiver.

papers.title: A Large Eddy Simulation Study of Turbine Pitch Motion Effects on Power Generation in Fully Developed Floating Wind Turbine Arrays
papers.abstract: Interactions between floating wind turbines and the marine atmospheric boundary layer affect turbine wakes and power output. This study examines the impact of turbine representations and platform pitching motion on power predictions for aligned floating wind turbine arrays. Large-eddy simulations (LES) are performed for a fully developed wind turbine array boundary layer with periodic streamwise and spanwise boundary conditions and moving surface drag (MOSD) at the bottom surface. A proposed power-curve-aware extension of the conventional actuator disk model (PCADM) is compared with the traditional constant coefficient actuator disk model (CCADM), which is valid in principle only during Region 2 operation. Harmonic pitching motion matched to a representative ocean wave frequency is prescribed for IEA 15MW turbines mounted on the UMaine VolturnUS-S platform. Results demonstrate that the CCADM produces unphysical power overshoot when relative velocities induced by harmonic pitching periodically exceed rated speed, while the PCADM eliminates these unrealistic excursions from the actual turbine operating range. Various wind-wave conditions and relative pitching motions for an aligned farm with PCADM turbines are analyzed, including in-phase, opposite-phase, and incommensurate-phase row-to-row relative turbine motion. Results reveal that, depending on operational regions, turbine pitching motion can either increase or decrease mean turbine power output. Among the relative phases considered, in-phase motions produce larger fluctuations at the farm scale due to stronger turbine-turbine correlations. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for turbine motion and associated changes in operational regions when modeling turbine and wind farm power production in LES of offshore floating wind farms using actuator disk representations.

papers.title: TIDE: A Physically Diverse 3D Turbulence Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Scientific Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Turbulence is a central testbed for machine learning on physical dynamics because its governing laws are known exactly. However, most existing studies remain in 2D, while 3D turbulence has fundamentally different physics and is far more costly to simulate. Existing 3D resources also typically provide only one realization per configuration, making it difficult to distinguish learning the dynamics from fitting the statistics of a single flow. In this paper, we introduce TIDE (Turbulent Incompressible DNS Ensembles), a 256^3 DNS corpus and benchmark for 3D incompressible turbulence, with 15 configurations on eight controlled axes, independent ensembles, pressure fields, and equation-level verification. The benchmark includes five tasks, standardized learned baselines, controlled generalization splits, and physical-fidelity metrics alongside pointwise error. Across the main forecasting configurations, current learned models barely outperform persistence and still make about twice the error of a spectral solver given the true equations. Moreover, lower pointwise error can coincide with severely distorted small-scale dynamics, showing that accuracy alone does not ensure physical fidelity. Generalization results further show that most regime shifts reflect limited training coverage, whereas forced-to-decay transfer exposes a missing conditioning variable: operators trained under forcing continue to predict driven evolution when the external drive is removed. Closing these accuracy, fidelity, and conditioning gaps is the central open problem made measurable by TIDE.

papers.title: Analysis of Nonlinear Phase Noise in Coherent Fiber-Optic Systems Based on Phase Shift Keying
papers.abstract: Analytical expressions for the phase variance in a nonlinear fiber optic system based on phase-shift keying are developed. The Gauss-Hermite functions are used as the orthogonal basis to represent the noise field. Number of degrees of freedom (DOF) to accurately model the phase variance is estimated. The amplifier noise excites higher order Gauss-Hermite noise modes and the nonlinear mixing of a signal pulse and higher order Gauss-Hermite noise mode leads to new noise fields which enhance the nonlinear phase noise. The higher order noise modes propagate linearly and enhance the linear phase noise if the matched filter is not used at the receiver. Analytical expression for the optimum launch power is developed taking into account the linear and nonlinear phase noise.

papers.title: An Artificial-Compressibility Physics-Informed Neural Network for the Unsteady Incompressible Navier--Stokes Equations
papers.abstract: We study a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for the unsteady, two-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equations in which the stiff divergence-free constraint is replaced by an artificial-compressibility (AC) relaxation governed by a single scalar parameter $\eps$. The relaxation reintroduces a pressure time derivative, converting a differential-algebraic constraint into an ordinary residual that a PINN can minimise directly. On the Taylor--Green vortex, which admits a closed-form unsteady solution, we quantify the effect of $\eps$: the residual divergence scales as $\eps\,|\partial_t p|$, so larger $\eps$ raises both the divergence and the velocity error, and both decrease monotonically and saturate as $\eps$ is reduced. On the $Re=100$ cylinder wake the plain forward AC-PINN collapses to the steady symmetric branch and does not reproduce von Kármán shedding; assimilating a few hundred sparse velocity sensors from a boundary-layer-resolved finite-element reference (whose Strouhal number, $0.176$, we bring close to the $0.164$--$0.172$ literature band by resolving the separating shear layer, though it remains just above it) recovers the unsteady vortex street to $7\%$ over the wake and its shedding frequency to within $3\%$ of that same reference --- a bound set by the reference's own fidelity rather than an independent validation against the true flow.

papers.title: Floquet stability analysis of pulsatile particle-laden channel flow
papers.abstract: We investigate the linear stability of particle-laden pulsatile channel flow using Floquet analysis within a two-phase dusty-gas framework. Uniformly distributed spherical particles are coupled to an incompressible Newtonian fluid through Stokes drag, and the governing equations are linearized about a time-periodic base flow driven by a sinusoidally varying pressure gradient. The effects of Reynolds number, Womersley number, pulsation amplitude, particle relaxation time, and particle mass fraction on temporal instability are examined. In the steady limit, particles with very short relaxation times destabilize the flow, whereas finite relaxation times introduce interphase slip and drag-mediated damping that stabilize disturbances. Under pulsatile forcing, increasing pulsation amplitude destabilizes the flow at low Womersley numbers but stabilizes it at sufficiently high Womersley numbers. This transition is governed by the penetration depth of oscillatory motion and is systematically shifted by particle relaxation time and mass loading through interphase momentum exchange. A critical corresponding value remains small throughout, indicating strong particle-fluid coupling and ruling out resonance-like particle dynamics. These findings provide a unified physical framework for the stability of pulsatile particle-laden flows relevant to physiological and periodically forced multiphase systems.

papers.title: Impact of Wind Direction on Flow and Turbulent Statistics Over a Realistic Urban Area: A Large-Eddy Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Effects of wind direction in realistic urban canopies remain difficult to characterize systematically because local flow patterns, building-height variability, and turbulent statistics within a realistic urban canopy may respond differently to changes in the approaching wind. To investigate these multi-scale directional impacts, we conducted high-resolution large-eddy simulations of the atmospheric boundary layer over the Zona Universitaria Pedralbes district in Barcelona. The computational meshes employ fourth-order spectral elements, yielding pedestrian-level resolutions below 1 m and resulting in approximately 5.0e8 degrees of freedom. Sixteen wind directions uniformly distributed over 360deg are simulated to capture the full directional response of the urban fabric.

papers.title: An optical-fibre-integrated buffer for packet-switched quantum networks
papers.abstract: Packet-switched quantum networks require buffers that can delay qubit payloads while routing information is read out in real time. Previous approaches have not provided this functionality in a fully fibre-integrated architecture compatible with telecom infrastructure. Here we demonstrate an optical-fibre-integrated buffer, based on a recirculating loop and a fibre storage line, in which the storage time of a polarisation-encoded qubit payload is determined by readout of an attached packet header. The key component behind this achievement is an ultra-low-loss poled fibre phase modulator, which provides fast, polarisation-insensitive switching directly in fibre and allows header and payload to be processed within the buffer. We demonstrate storage and retrieval of polarisation-encoded qubit payloads for storage times up to 47 $μ$s, with an average quantum bit error rate of 1.8% together with stable operation over several hours. These results establish a practical fibre-based architecture for packet-level quantum network buffering that can easily integrate into the current telecommunication infrastructure opening up new paths for deployment of the quantum internet.

papers.title: Structured light under turbulence
papers.abstract: Structured light has emerged as a promising resource for high-capacity and secure free-space optical communication, where atmospheric turbulence remains a major source of signal degradation. In this work, we investigate the resilience of different transverse mode structures of an optical beam with respect to the random action of turbulence. A spatial light modulator (SLM) is programmed to apply amplitude and phase modulation corresponding to the desired transverse mode, which is then transmitted through a turbulent medium emulated by a second SLM. Laguerre-Gauss, Hermite-Gauss, and Airy beams are investigated through the resulting intensity distributions measured with a camera. Different figures of merit are used to evaluate and compare the resilience of these modes.

papers.title: The Most Dangerous Seed: Nonlinear Optimal Perturbations in Rayleigh-Taylor Instability
papers.abstract: Long-term instabilities in astrophysical fluids are inherently nonlinear, where even small-amplitude perturbations can trigger dramatic instability. However, owing to the complex interactions among non-normal modes, the perturbation structures responsible for the greatest growth remain poorly understood. In this paper, we employ the nonlinear optimization method known as the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) to identify the most dangerous initial velocity perturbation, i.e., the perturbation that maximizes the kinetic energy growth in the two-dimensional compressible Rayleigh-Taylor instability in astrophysical hydrodynamics. Compared with random perturbations, the optimal perturbation forms a coherent wave-packet structure localized around the density interface. We investigate its dependence on spatial resolution and optimization time horizon through two sets of numerical experiments. For a fixed optimization time, increasing the spatial resolution produces a more sharply localized wave packet, whereas for a fixed spatial resolution, increasing the optimization time causes the wave packet to become progressively more dispersed. Furthermore, we analyze the optimal perturbations in Fourier space using the fast Fourier transform (FFT), which provides a clearer characterization of the spectral distribution. Higher-resolution simulations concentrate most of the perturbation energy into only a few dominant modes, while longer optimization times distribute the energy over a broader range of modes. These results indicate that short optimization time horizons involve relatively weak modal interactions and remain closer to the linear regime, whereas longer optimization times enhance nonlinear modal interactions, broaden the spectral distribution, and reduce the predictive capability of linear stability theory.

papers.title: Localizing polymers promotes the centre-mode elastic instability
papers.abstract: The centre-mode elastic instability, prevalent in rectilinear flows of dilute polymer solutions, allows dynamic states to emerge even in the absence of inertia. Here, we show that this instability can be significantly enhanced when the base flow has a nonuniform spatial-distribution of polymers. In such a flow, the polymeric stress not only depends on the conformation tensor (determined here by the Oldroyd-B equation) but also varies proportionally with the polymer concentration field, which satisfies a scalar transport equation. Focusing on the inertialess Stokes limit, we first consider the simple setting of periodic Kolmogorov flow. A linear stability analysis shows that a nonuniform polymer concentration either promotes or suppresses the centre-mode instability, depending on whether the polymers are localised near or away from the maximum of the base-velocity profile. We then focus on a base flow with a distinct polymer-laden stream overlying the base-velocity maximum, and sandwiched between polymer-free streams. We find that the critical Weissenberg number (product of the elastic relaxation time and the typical strain-rate) at the onset of instability undergoes a sudden decrease as the total polymer loading is increased. An energy analysis attributes this destabilisation to elastic feedback forces that arise from concentration gradients near the interfaces between the polymer-laden and polymer-free streams. The insights from Kolmogorov flow are shown to carry over to channel flow, where localising polymers about the centreline strongly promotes the centre-mode instability.

papers.title: Refraction laws in spatio-temporal media
papers.abstract: We study the time-dependent Maxwell system, formulated in the sense of distributions, for electromagnetic waves propagating through media with temporal and spatial material interfaces. Under explicit trace and regularity assumptions on the permittivity and permeability, we derive the jump conditions produced by temporal discontinuities and by subsequent spatial interfaces. These conditions are used to obtain generalized Snell laws for the wave vectors generated by temporal splitting, reflection, and transmission. We also derive the associated amplitude equations and organize them as a finite-dimensional linear system for a space-time slab geometry. Finally, we provide an explicit oblique-incidence example. Our approach does not impose a smooth-field ansatz and allows material parameters that need not be constant away from the interfaces.

papers.title: Can crystal symmetry reshape ENZ photonics?: Opinion
papers.abstract: Over the last decade, epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) photonics has been driven by the search for lower losses and stronger nonlinear responses. Here, I ask a different question: can crystal symmetry also be used to shape the ENZ response? I focus on low-symmetry conductors, where the geometry of the electronic states can produce electric currents that are not present in ordinary Drude materials. These currents may enable polarization-dependent gain, nonreciprocal effects, and ultrafast nonlinearities controlled by symmetry and an external bias. I suggest that such materials may be useful for active and time-varying nanophotonics.

papers.title: Symmetry/asymmetry within a cylindrical lattice model of nuclear structure predicts cosmic abundance/scarcity
papers.abstract: Protons and neutrons are the smallest forms of measurable matter, and each nucleon has 3 up (+2/3) and down (-1/3) quarks. Quarks treated as point-like particles within polygonal geometries model the structures of stable nuclides through $^{36}$Ar. The model derives from the proton's radius (r=0.8414 fm), the hadron's prolate spheroid shape (from the $Δ(1232)$ resonance), and the separation distance between bound nucleons ($\approx$0.8 fm, from the Argonne $v_{18}$ $NN$ potential). The prolate nucleon's spatial extent arises from its 3 quarks, which implies a qualitatively linear quark sequence. Spin-spin forces repel the like-flavored quarks to opposite ends of the nucleon, leaving the unlike quark in the middle. Quark-to-quark distance within the nucleon corresponds to the nucleon's radius. Nucleons link by quark-to-quark interactions to form proton-neutron short-range correlated pairs (pn SRC pairs), separated by a distance equal to the proton's radius. Alternating nucleons produce regularly alternating up/down quark sequences. We contemplate structures for each stable nuclide through $^{36}$Ar and include the one whose rotational radius (from the regular polygon radius formula) best correlates with its accepted charge radius (r(31)=0.98, p<0.001). Nucleon alternation makes pn SRC pairs and produces the equal numbers of protons and neutrons (Z=N) in the isotopes $^{4}_{2}$He, $^{12}_{6}$C, $^{14}_{7}$N, $^{16}_{8}$O, $^{20}_{10}$Ne, $^{24}_{12}$Mg, $^{28}_{14}$Si, and $^{32}_{16}$S, comprising 99.5% of stable baryonic matter. Bilateral structural symmetry emerges as a sensitive and specific predictor of cosmic abundance. Opposing deuteron-deuteron alternating quark charge sequences produce alternating and unequal electromagnetic fields capable of modelling the close-range attraction and far-range repulsion of the fusion potential curve and Coulomb potential energy barrier.

papers.title: Modulation in degree of cross-polarization at Young's interferometer illuminated by non-uniformly polarized electromagnetic fields
papers.abstract: The degree of cross-polarization (DoCP) and the electromagnetic degree of coherence (EM DoC) of an electromagnetic beam are investigated at the observation points for incoherent and non-uniformly polarized, i.e., different degree of polarization with respect to space at the two pinholes in Young's interference experiment. We note that DoCP at the observation plane can be expressed as the average value of the degree of polarization at the pinholes of Young's interference experiment. The present study also verifies that the DoCP is a two-point generalization of the DoP. Additionally, EM DoC at observation points can be controlled by DoP at pinholes. The findings may be useful for classical ghost imaging, lensless imaging, and the study of Stokes correlations.

papers.title: Joint spectral characterization of SPDC photon pairs near 2 $μ$m in (Al)GaAs-on-insulator waveguides
papers.abstract: Integrated photon-pair sources are a core component of chip-based quantum computing, communication, and metrology. Although such sources have been demonstrated at conventional telecom wavelengths, the 2 $μ$m band remains comparatively less explored, despite offering advantages for free-space quantum communication, low-loss transmission in emerging fiber networks, and integration with silicon photonic platforms. In this paper, we demonstrate spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in straight GaAs- and AlGaAs-on-insulator waveguides. This platform offers strong second-order nonlinearity and geometry-tunable dispersion, which are advantageous for efficient on-chip pair generation. Measurements of the joint spectral intensity and heralded second-order correlation function show broadband emission around 2 $μ$m with strong spectral anti-correlations. To our knowledge, this is the first direct joint-spectral characterization of an integrated SPDC source in this wavelength regime.

papers.title: Self-Focusing Control for Depth-Precise Wafer Slicing of 4H-SiC in Femtosecond Laser Processing
papers.abstract: 4H-SiC has emerged as a third-generation chip material because its superior thermal conductivity and high breakdown field enable the material to achieve high power density and higher switching frequencies in power-electronics applications. As chip architectures evolve toward 3D and heterogeneous integration, the mechanical and thermal design space tightens while yield risks grow. In particular, advanced packages require mid-process wafer thinning to < 100 $μ$m to shorten interconnects and control thermo-mechanical stress. Femtosecond laser slicing for 4H-SiC wafers offers a non-contact processing approach to produce thin layers with low defects, while strong optical nonlinearities obscure the relationship between the laser parameters and the resulting slicing quality. Here, we systematically investigate Kerr-induced self-focusing using a femtosecond laser in 4H-SiC slicing by combining experiments, a semi-empirical analytical model, and numerical ray optics simulations. We demonstrate that the interplay between pulse energy and processing depth governs the self-focusing behavior, which directly correlates with post-separation surface texture parameters and separation stress, thereby linking nonlinear beam propagation to slicing quality. Based on this relationship, we define a processability map in the pulse energy with self-focusing depth space over a normalized irradiance background. Analytically, the model extends the Marburger formula to focused beams by replacing the power ratio with a normalized irradiance. Ray optics simulations capture the geometric features at the self-focusing point and are validated against experimental observations. Within physically defined thresholds, the processability map directly connects laser parameters to separation stress and surface texture metrics, providing practical guidance for depth control beyond trial-and-error.

papers.title: Educational approach to general relativity through its approximate vectorial form
papers.abstract: General Relativity (GR) can be effectively examined in the low-velocity, weak-field limit, where its inherently tensorial structure simplifies to a vector-based formulation closely analogous to classical electrodynamics. This correspondence becomes particularly clear when both theories are expressed within a field-free, interaction-based framework, in which the leading relativistic corrections emerge naturally as velocity- and acceleration-dependent modifications to the static interaction. As a result, several predictions of GR can be derived using familiar techniques from electrodynamics, provided the relevant phenomena remain within the regime of validity of the approximation. This structural analogy facilitates a conceptual understanding of GR enabling the introduction of its core ideas even in an introductory level course, the single exception being the treatment of radiation, which requires tools at more advanced level. Building on this pedagogical framework, the incorporation of special relativity (SR) and the equivalence principle enables concise and transparent derivations of gravitational time dilation, as well as its immediate consequences, including light deflection and gravitational frequency shifts. A detailed exposition of this material is provided in the supplementary material.

papers.title: AFLOW-EMERALD: ElectroMagnetic modes EngineeRing in Advanced LayereD materials
papers.abstract: Layered and periodically patterned heterostructures underpin advanced optical, photonic, and plasmonic (meta)materials, whose rational design demands electromagnetic solvers that are both numerically robust and tightly linked to the underlying material properties. Here, we present AFLOW-EMERALD (ElectroMagnetic modes EngineeRing in Advanced LayereD materials), an open-source, modular, Python-based computational framework for simulating electromagnetic wave propagation in finite and periodic layered (meta)materials. Built around a unified object-oriented architecture, AFLOW-EMERALD combines a numerically stable scattering-matrix method with plane-wave expansion and extends to rigorous coupled-wave analysis for laterally patterned structures such as gratings. The software computes optical spectra, spatial field distributions, and photonic band structures, including complex-k dispersion in lossy, dispersive media. A streamlined YAML workflow allows users to seamlessly import dielectric function datasets from experimental, literature, or first-principles sources. Owing to its modular design, AFLOW-EMERALD is readily extensible and suitable for integration into computational materials-design pipelines, providing a practical platform for the coupled material-geometry engineering of dielectric photonic crystals, plasmonic multilayers, hyperbolic metamaterials, and more complex architectures supporting, e.g., surface and volume plasmon-polariton modes.

papers.title: Fully Distributed Fiber-Optic Sensing Enabled by Kalman Filtering
papers.abstract: Signal fading creates points along the fiber where phase cannot be extracted, so they are conventionally discarded. Instead, we propose a Kalman-based solution for φ-OTDR full-fiber monitoring. Experiments demonstrate phase and temperature estimation with approximately 15 times better spatial density than if removing these points.

papers.title: A windy sea surface with Stokes waves
papers.abstract: Predicting the transition of wind-forced, gravito-capillary surface waves from smooth to corrugated states remains a longstanding problem in nonlinear surface wave mechanics. Solving driven-dissipative, nonlinear potential flow equations we map these waves ($4-13$ cm) onto a Reynolds number -- wave energy phase-space. We identify a transition band separating smooth from corrugated wave states - the wave steepness exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on Reynolds number within this. Subharmonic (in)stability analysis reveals that the fastest-growing mode intensifies corrugations on alternate faces of the carrier wave. Our results offer insights into parasitic capillary wave formation on steep carrier waves and are of interest to ocean remote-sensing.

papers.title: Analysis of Moment Closures Using $\varphi$-Divergences for Rarefied Dynamics with Binary Collisions and Their Galerkin Discretizations
papers.abstract: This work introduces a robust deterministic framework for approximating solutions of the Boltzmann equation with binary collisions by discretizing their dependence on time, position, and velocity using Galerkin methods. By employing a family of parametric Galerkin closures based on $\varphi$-divergences in velocity space, we derive rigorous hierarchies of moment equations that govern fluid dynamic variables. Addressing the limitation that these closures alone do not guarantee dissipation of a $\varphi$-divergence entropy for the true binary collision operator, we restore this property by formulating a compatible approximate collision operator tailored to each closure. This constructed operator intrinsically retains fundamental physical properties essential for high-fidelity flow simulations, including Galilean invariance, exact conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, and strict dissipation of a $\varphi$-divergence entropy. Furthermore, we show that the resulting closed moment systems are symmetric-dissipative, yielding Cauchy problems that are well-posed locally in time. To translate this mathematical foundation into an efficient computational tool, we discretize the position and time variables with an entropy-stable discontinuous Galerkin (DG) finite element method. The fully implicit, entropy-stable space-time approach enables time steps far beyond typical CFL-limited step sizes and the direct computation of steady states. The robustness and accuracy of the methodology are verified and validated through numerical simulations on the supersonic nozzle flow of argon, mass flow through a channel, and heat transfer between parallel walls, demonstrating agreement with analytical benchmarks, experimental measurements, and stochastic particle simulations.

papers.title: A 100x Faster Beam Propagation Method for Nonlinear Optical Wave Propagation Based on Discrete Exterior Calculus
papers.abstract: Efficient simulation of nonlinear light propagation in complex photonic structures remains a major challenge because these systems combine intricate transverse geometries with propagation over distances spanning many diffraction lengths. Existing numerical methods often require computationally intensive uniform discretizations or struggle to accurately represent complex material boundaries, limiting the practical simulation of multiscale nonlinear photonic devices. Here we introduce a computational framework for solving the nonlinear Schrödinger equation that accelerates simulations by more than two orders of magnitude (over 100x) compared with conventional approaches while maintaining spectral-level accuracy, thereby reducing the computational time required to solve large-scale and multiscale problems from days to hours. The method is based on discrete exterior calculus, enabling geometry-conforming discretization directly on unstructured meshes without the weak formulations required by conventional finite-element methods. In contrast to Fourier-based spectral solvers, it avoids global oversampling, eliminates Gibbs-type oscillations at material interfaces, naturally incorporates absorbing boundary conditions, and preserves the topological structure of the underlying differential operators. A key feature of the framework is that higher-order propagation operators are generated algorithmically from lower-order discrete operators, providing a systematic route to extending simulations beyond the standard nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Benchmarks on fundamental solitons, asymmetric beams, and optical vortices confirm spectral-level accuracy while demonstrating computational speedups exceeding 100x.

papers.title: Generation and Enhancement of Bipartite and Tripartite Entanglement in an Electro-Optomechanical Ring Cavity
papers.abstract: This study investigates the generation and enhancement of quantum entanglement in an electro-optomechanical ring cavity system. The setup integrates two Coulomb-coupled mechanical resonators, which serve as the fundamental mechanism for the generation of bipartite and tripartite entanglement via charge mediated coupling. We then demonstrate the significant enhancement of this entanglement via a nonlinear parametric drive (an optical parametric amplifier, OPA), which injects a controllable nonlinearity into the cavity. We derive the system's Hamiltonian and the corresponding quantum Langevin equations, which are linearized around steady-state solutions to analyze Gaussian quantum fluctuations. Employing the covariance matrix formalism, we quantify bipartite entanglement via logarithmic negativity and tripartite entanglement via the minimum residual contangle. Our results unequivocally show that while the Coulomb interaction is indispensable for creating entanglement, the OPA acts as a powerful control tool, dramatically amplifying the degree of quantum correlations for all subsystems. We find that the strength of entanglement is highly sensitive to several parameters and can be optimized through the strategic selection of the OPA's gain and phase, the laser detuning, and the input power. A key finding is the existence of a trade-off, where parameters that maximize entanglement also constrain the stable operating regime of the system. Furthermore, thermal noise is shown to progressively degrade all quantum correlations, underscoring the necessity for low-temperature operation. These findings provide comprehensive guidance for parameter optimization, outlining a clear path from generation to enhancement, and highlight the potential of such hybrid systems as versatile platforms for controlling multipartite entanglement in quantum technologies.

papers.title: AOM-based ultra-low noise laser intensity control up to the MHz range
papers.abstract: High-power laser sources that exhibit low relative intensity noise and allow simultaneous dynamic control of their light level are required for a broad range of applications in various fields of physics. Acousto-optic modulators (AOMs) are widely used for active power stabilization and regulation due to their simple drive electronics requirements and high optical power handling capability in free-space. However, the rather slow propagation speed of the sound wave within the AOM crystal typically limits their control bandwidth to a few hundred kHz. In this work, we present a novel AOM-based control system that is capable of significantly suppressing intensity noise of high-power lasers up to the MHz range. By combining two standard feedback loops with one feedforward control branch and optimizing the beam path in the AOM crystal, ultra-low relative intensity noise levels down to $-155\, \text{dB}\,\text{Hz}^{-1}$ even at several hundred kHz are achieved. Our results are relevant for applications that require ultra-low intensity noise at Fourier frequencies up to the MHz range, such as optical lattice experiments with light ultracold atoms.

papers.title: Modelisation of chaotic systems with a latent Stochastic Differential Equation
papers.abstract: Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) have become a cornerstone of scientific machine learning, though they are predominantly utilized as algorithmic tools for uncertainty quantification or distribution matching. In contrast, leveraging SDEs fundamentally to model macroscopic, nonlinear physics as stochastic processes remains largely unexplored. This work introduces a probabilistic, non-intrusive reduced-order model (ROM) for chaotic dynamical systems. We argue that projecting high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics onto a low-dimensional manifold introduces irreducible uncertainty, compounded by the chaotic attractors and multi-admissible futures inherent to turbulent flows. Consequently, a chaotic system governed by a partial differential equation can be effectively modeled by an SDE in a suitable latent space. To this end, a nonlinear autoencoder is employed to map the flow field into a low-dimensional representation, within which the temporal evolution is explicitly governed by an SDE. The predictable component of the dynamics is captured by a learned drift term, while state-dependent stochasticity is absorbed by a diffusion term. We demonstrate that this probabilistic framework successfully propagates highly nonlinear states, offering a robust alternative to traditional deterministic methodologies for chaotic regimes. Ultimately, our model generates new chaotic flow trajectories that remain locally and globally consistent with the true transition kernel learned from Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) data. Even though these generated trajectories are unique and distinct from the training set, they preserve the underlying statistics and manifolds, validating the strong generative performance and robustness of our methodology.

papers.title: Mesoscopic Quantum Communication via Photon-Number Moments
papers.abstract: Mesoscopic optical states are a promising resource for quantum communication, combining robustness against losses with the preservation of genuine quantum features. Here, we propose a quantum communication protocol in which information is encoded in the first and second moments of the photon-number distributions of classical optical states, and then decoded by photon-number-resolving detectors. Security relies on the nonclassical photon-number correlations of a twin-beam state transmitted alongside the signal in the quantum channel, providing an experimentally accessible security witness against both intercept-resend and beam-splitter attacks investigated in this work. Numerical simulations performed in experimentally accessible parameter regimes support the feasibility and security of the proposed communication protocol, yielding nonzero key generation rates under the considered eavesdropping attacks, and motivating its future experimental implementation.

papers.title: On-chip Quantum Measurement of Squeezing Generated from a Silicon Nitride Micro-ring Resonator
papers.abstract: Integration of quantum optical technique on-chip is crucial for large scale applications of quantum technology, which were proven in a free space environment to be superior to the corresponding classical technology. Squeezed states of light can be used for enhancing the sensitivity of quantum sensors and for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Although chip-based squeezed light generation has advanced significantly, practical impact remains limited because coupling losses between the chip and off-chip detectors destroy delicate quantum correlations, restricting the amount of observed squeezing. Here, we overcome this limitation by implementing the idea of on-chip quantum measurement with the aid of a parametric amplifier and applying it to the squeezed state generated by a silicon nitride (SiN) microring resonator. In our scheme, two matched SiN micro-rings are sequentially constructed. The first ring generates a squeezed state, whereas the second ring acts as a high-gain parametric amplifier (PA) that measures the squeezed state before the light experiences significant off-chip loss. This architecture is inherently loss-tolerant: the amplifier elevates the quantum noise well above the vacuum level, making the measurement insensitive to downstream losses. We directly observe a quantum noise reduction of 4.6 dB from the first ring, despite a chip-to-fiber coupling loss exceeding 5 dB. This work also demonstrates the first monolithic SU(1,1) interferometer with an estimated 5 dB signal-to-noise enhancement compared to traditional linear interferometers, and thus establishes a practical pathway for chip-based quantum sensors.

papers.title: Mid-infrared spontaneous and stimulated emission dynamics in black phosphorus
papers.abstract: Black phosphorus (BP) has attracted attention as a light-emitting layered semiconductor for mid-infrared (MIR) photonics owing to its direct and thickness-tunable bandgap energy, highly anisotropic optical transitions, and potentially suppressed Auger recombination. However, spontaneous and stimulated emission dynamics governed by carrier recombination in BP have remained unexplored because time-resolved emission spectroscopy is challenging in the MIR region. Here we develop a time-resolved MIR emission microscope combining wavelength upconversion with superconducting single photon detection. This approach enables observation of emission dynamics in photoexcited BP at a wavelength around 4.6 μm with sub-100-ps temporal resolution. Temperature-dependent measurements reveal a crossover from excitonic to electron-hole plasma emission at around 70 K, supported by independent results in the characteristic transition temperature, pump-fluence dependence, and rise and decay dynamics of MIR emission. In a suspended BP structure, we further observe a nonlinear increase in the emission intensity above a well-defined pump threshold. Spectral narrowing and intense picosecond emission pulses appear above the threshold, providing solid evidence of stimulated emission assisted by optical feedback from a Fabry-Pérot cavity. These results elucidate ultrafast carrier dynamics and optical gain formation in BP and establish time-resolved upconversion spectroscopy as a powerful approach for investigating MIR photonic materials and devices.

papers.title: Event-Based Spatial-Carrier Interferometry for Surface-Normal Vibration-Waveform Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Non-contact measurement of small vibrations perpendicular to a surface supports the evaluation of mechanical structures, but in camera-based interferometry, increasing the frame rate makes a trade-off with the field of view and spatial resolution. By recording only brightness changes, event cameras avoid this trade-off and reach high temporal and spatial resolution; our previously reported event topology-based visual vibrometer recovers vibration from apparent motion. This high-speed, high-resolution sensing is well suited to full-field measurement, yet such vibration produces too little apparent motion to capture its waveform. Here we show that event-based spatial-carrier interferometry reconstructs that waveform from moving interference fringes.
